title: Unknown Fields Lost During Partial-Schema Read–Modify–Write
pattern: Code decodes an external or stored record using a type that recognizes only some fields, discards the rest, and serializes that partial representation back as the replacement record or as a payload that is supposed to be forwarded losslessly.
why_bad: Older or narrower consumers silently remove schema extensions written by newer versions, breaking forward compatibility and causing data loss during rolling deployments or mixed-version read-write loops.
detection: Trace deserialization into a fixed local schema through modification and re-encoding to the same record/source (e.g. a full-document overwrite of the row it was read from) or through a forwarding path. Establish that replacement semantics discard unrecognized keys and that no serializer support, catch-all buffer (such as a `#[serde(flatten)]` map), or field-level update preserves them. Deriving both `Deserialize` and `Serialize` alone does not establish a destructive round trip.
fix:
Preserve unrecognized data through the entire decode/encode path using the format's unknown-field support or an appropriate catch-all representation, such as `#[serde(flatten)]` with a JSON-value map for compatible object formats, or update only the intended fields (e.g. `UPDATE ... SET`) instead of replacing the whole record. Preserve unknown data at every relevant nested level and keep explicit known-field update/conflict semantics; a top-level buffer is not sufficient if nested records are destructively decoded.
```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

#[derive(serde::Deserialize, serde::Serialize)]
struct PersonV1 {
    user_name: String,
    favorite_number: u64,
    #[serde(flatten)]
    extra_fields: HashMap<String, serde_json::Value>, // preserves unknown fields
}
```
source: *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* by Martin Kleppmann (2017), Chapter 4, p. 125, Figure 4-7; *Vaughn Vernon - Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013)*, Chapter 14.
